audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 1 Kings / Melakhim Aleph chapter 5, first-pass draft aligned to public-domain verse structure; formal witness audit remains required.
audit_status.review_note: Reviewed for Tyrian diplomacy, cedar extraction, Sidonian expertise, food exchange, covenant, conscription, rotational labor, burden carriers, quarry workers, supervisors, and monumental construction.

verses.restored: Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon, for he heard they had anointed him king in place of his father; Hiram had loved David all days.
You know David my father could not build a house for name of YHWH his Divine because of wars surrounding him, until YHWH put them beneath soles of his feet.
But now YHWH my Divine has given me rest from every side; there is no adversary and no evil occurrence.
Look, I intend to build a house for name of YHWH my Divine, as YHWH spoke to David my father: Your son whom I place upon your throne in your place—he shall build house for my name.

Now command that cedars be cut for me from Lebanon. My servants shall be with your servants, and I will give wages for your servants according to all you say, for you know no one among us knows how to cut timber like Sidonians.
When Hiram heard Solomon's words, he rejoiced greatly and said, Blessed be YHWH this day, who gave David a wise son over this great people.
Hiram sent to Solomon: I heard what you sent to me. I will do all your desire concerning cedar timber and cypress timber.

My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon to sea. I will make them into rafts by sea to place you appoint, break them apart there, and you shall take them. You shall do my desire by providing food for my household.
Hiram gave Solomon cedar and cypress timber according to all his desire.
Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household and twenty kors of beaten oil; Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.
YHWH gave Solomon wisdom as promised. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two cut a covenant.
King Solomon raised forced labor from all Israel; levy was thirty thousand men.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts, ten thousand per month: one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was over forced labor.
Solomon had seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters in mountain,
besides Solomon's chief officers over work, three thousand three hundred who ruled over people doing work.
The king commanded, and they quarried great stones, costly stones, hewn stones, to lay foundation of house.
Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and Gebalites shaped them; they prepared timber and stones to build house.

translation_notes: Hiram and Sidonian workers bring specialized maritime and timber knowledge. Their expertise must not be reduced to foreign labor serving Israel's glory.
The cedar trade transforms Lebanon's forests into royal sacred architecture. Ecological cost and sovereignty over natural resources remain ethical questions.
Solomon describes peace as absence of adversaries, then uses that peace to mobilize enormous compulsory labor. Rest from war is not rest for workers.
Thirty thousand Israelites rotate into Lebanon, while seventy thousand carry burdens and eighty thousand cut stone. Monumental worship is built through bodies, time, family separation, and danger.
The text distinguishes wages for Hiram's servants from Solomon's levy. This raises labor-status, compensation, and coercion questions that later become central to the kingdom's fracture.
Covenant between kings does not reveal whether workers or affected communities consented to the terms.
Large, costly stones symbolize permanence, but sacred permanence cannot justify exploitation or worker deaths.
safety_note: Do not romanticize forced labor, ecological extraction, imperial building, or elite treaties as automatically holy. A house for YHWH must be evaluated by the treatment, consent, compensation, rest, and safety of those who build it.
